text:
The first thing Miss Emily gave me was a receipt. It was for a navy wool coat she had bought on my behalf, and she folded it into my hand while her son stood beside the department-store mirror, smiling as though we had accomplished something.

“In case the sleeves aren’t right,” she said.

The sleeves were right. Everything about the coat was right except that it belonged to someone who would have known where to wear it.

I had been married to her son for eleven days.

Before that, I had been a cashier at Bell’s Market, where we wore red aprons and were not permitted to sit. I knew the codes for forty-three varieties of produce and could distinguish a jar breaking from a bottle breaking without turning around. A bottle made a hopeful sound first.

Daniel called this my eye, although generally my ear or my feet had supplied the information. He designed the interiors of public buildings. At dinner he sometimes described a staircase as generous.

We met when his card was declined at my register.

In his telling, this became a story about my kindness. I split his groceries between two cards after he exceeded a daily spending limit buying a bicycle. In mine, it was about a man who hadn’t known how much money he was allowed to spend.

Both versions omitted the woman behind him, holding a frozen turkey against her hip.

We married four months later, on a Thursday. There was no emergency. Daniel said that if we intended to do it, delaying was a kind of superstition. This struck me as sophisticated reasoning. It also struck me that I loved him.

We told his mother that evening. She was in Milwaukee, inspecting a laundry she might buy.

Daniel put her on speaker.

“Well,” she said.

He took my hand.

“Well,” she said again. “Let me find somewhere to sit.”

***

Everyone called her Miss Emily, including people older than she was. Her surname was Voss, but Miss Voss sounded like a substitute teacher, she said, and Mrs. Voss was Daniel’s dead grandmother.

I called her Emily once.

We were in her kitchen, a room with two sinks and no visible dish soap.

“Yes, please, Emily,” I said when she offered coffee.

She opened a cupboard. I heard the refrigerator stop humming.

“Of course, sweetheart.”

For weeks afterward, I avoided calling her anything.

Her husband had left when Daniel was nine. People described this as the year she started her business, though it had existed for three years already. What happened when he left was that she stopped pretending it was supplementary income.

She took hotel managers to lunch and drove delivery routes when drivers failed to appear. Daniel remembered sleeping on bags of clean tablecloths, a charming detail until he mentioned the detergent headaches.

By the time we met, she employed two hundred people. Her house had a room devoted to wrapping gifts. I had never encountered wealth in that form: the ability to prepare for occasions that hadn’t happened yet.

At a family lunch, Daniel’s aunt asked how we had found each other.

“At Bell’s,” I said. “I was working.”

“How lovely.”

“I was on register six.”

She smiled as though I had made a joke requiring kindness rather than comprehension.

Later, Miss Emily said, “You don’t have to give people your whole employment history.”

“I only gave her the location.”

“There’s nothing wrong with working at a market.”

“I know that, too.”

She looked up. For a moment, I thought she might like me better.

***

Daniel’s apartment occupied two floors above a dentist. Previously, I had shared a one-bedroom with my cousin Patrice and her daughter. At Daniel’s, the second bathroom contained only a towel and a plant. I sometimes went in just to understand it.

He suggested I stop working.

“What would I do?”

“Whatever you wanted.”

People who say this generally have a few things in mind.

I wanted my legs to stop aching. I wanted a dental cleaning without an argument about insurance. I wanted to take Patrice’s daughter to the aquarium and buy the sandwich shaped like a fish.

“You could go back to school,” he said.

I had left community college after my mother’s second surgery. Go back made it sound as though I had stepped outside to take a call.

I reduced my hours instead. On free afternoons, the apartment’s silence seemed to require an explanation. Sometimes I went downstairs and read magazines until the dentist’s receptionist asked whether I had an appointment.

When Miss Emily heard, she laughed.

“Come to the office,” she said. “We have magazines, too.”

***

The office was above her largest laundry. Inside, sheets traveled overhead on rails. A woman fed pillowcases into a machine that swallowed them with an animal’s indifference.

“This is Nora,” Miss Emily told people. “Daniel’s wife.”

She said wife firmly. I hadn’t realized how much I’d been waiting for that.

Upstairs, she asked what I had studied.

“Accounting. A little.”

“How little?”

“Three semesters.”

“That isn’t a little.”

“It’s not a degree.”

“No,” she said. “It isn’t.”

There was comfort in her refusal to improve a fact for my benefit.

She asked me to compare invoices with delivery records. I found a duplicate charge and a hotel billed for bath mats it didn’t use.

“Good,” she said. “Now tell me what we missed.”

The we pleased me so much that I resented it.

She offered me part-time work at four dollars an hour above Bell’s.

I asked for six.

“Why?”

I had expected generosity or offense. Having to produce a reason felt unfair, though I knew it wasn’t.

“Because you want someone who’ll tell you about the bath mats.”

“Five,” she said. “And a review in ninety days.”

***

Working for Miss Emily didn’t make her easier to visit.

At work, she was exact. At home, instructions arrived disguised as concern.

Was I warm enough in that dress? Had I meant to park so close to the gate? Did Daniel know I put wooden spoons in the dishwasher?

Once she watched me cut a pear.

“You’ll lose half of it.”

“It’s a pear.”

“Yes,” she said.

Daniel believed we were becoming friends. He had the dangerous confidence of a man who had never been responsible for the atmosphere in a room.

“She wants you to feel at home.”

“Then why keep telling me how things are done?”

“Because that’s what she knows how to talk about.”

It was an intelligent answer, which made it less useful.

His criticisms of her were established, worn smooth. She worked too much. She was controlling. He could pronounce her impossible and then call to ask which plumber to use.

I was still learning what each opinion might cost.

***

In January, Patrice called about overdue rent. Her pharmacy hours had been cut, and her daughter needed an inhaler, a fact she offered apologetically, as though the child had chosen an extravagant hobby.

I transferred nine hundred dollars from our shared account.

Daniel noticed that evening.

“We should discuss things like this.”

“You bought a chair last week.”

“The chair is for us.”

“So is Patrice being indoors.”

“I would have said yes.”

“Then I saved you some time.”

This wasn’t fair. It wasn’t entirely unfair either.

The next afternoon, Miss Emily asked me to close her office door.

“Daniel worries.”

“He seemed able to discuss it with you.”

She removed her glasses.

“You need an account of your own.”

“I have one.”

“With money in it.”

When Daniel’s father left, she said, their checking account contained seventy-three dollars. Payroll was due Friday. In photographs from that period, she looked remarkably thin.

“People kept telling me how well I looked.”

I prepared to refuse money without sounding proud or ungrateful.

Instead, she said, “Decide what belongs to the household and what belongs to each of you. Write it down. You don’t want to ask permission.”

“He told you I helped my cousin.”

“He did.”

“And you’re telling me how not to ask his permission.”

“I can think he was wrong to call me and still answer the telephone.”

***

In March, she invited me to a benefit at a hotel whose linen contract we had lost.

“Why are we going?”

“Because they might come back.”

Daniel was away. I wore the navy coat over a black dress I had bought myself. The dress had pockets, a private victory.

A man with pink eyelids asked whether I was her new assistant.

“My daughter-in-law.”

“Oh! Daniel’s bride.”

He examined me with the benevolence of someone inspecting another person’s purchase.

Miss Emily touched my back.

“Nora caught a billing error your purchasing department missed for six months.”

“Then we owe you one.”

“Several,” she said.

I loved her at that moment. The force of it embarrassed me.

At dinner, a woman asked what I had done before the laundry.

“I worked at Bell’s.”

“I love Bell’s. Those little oranges. What are they called?”

“Clementines?”

“No, the other ones.”

We spent a long time identifying fruit.

In the car, Miss Emily said, “You needn’t lead with the supermarket.”

“She asked.”

“You can say retail.”

“Would that have helped her find the oranges?”

She watched the road.

“You think I’m ashamed of you.”

“Are you?”

“No.”

“What are you trying to prevent?”

She stopped at a yellow light we could have made.

“People decide where to put you very quickly.”

“You want them to put me somewhere else.”

“I want you to have a moment before they decide.”

The heater clicked.

“I wasn’t unhappy every minute,” I said.

“At Bell’s?”

“In my life before.”

“I didn’t say you were.”

“No. But everybody’s so relieved.”

***

My first serious mistake involved a nursing home with two names. One appeared on the contract, the other on the building. I applied a payment to the wrong account and threatened suspension of service.

The administrator called Miss Emily.

She summoned me before lunch.

“Did you check the account number?”

“No. I recognized the name.”

“You recognized a name.”

She pushed the paperwork toward me.

“I’m sorry.”

“I know. Call him. Correct it. Then find out whether there are other accounts like this.”

Her tone was sharp, but no different from the one she used with the operations manager.

Still, when she called that evening about Sunday dinner, I nearly cried.

“Do you want us to come?”

“Why would I ask otherwise?”

I couldn’t explain that my family often offered things they hoped you would decline. Come stay awhile. Take the last piece. Want and capacity had to negotiate before anyone answered.

On Sunday, she served roast pork and discussed a movie. She never mentioned the account.

I had spent the weekend preparing to bear her displeasure. She appeared to have put it away.

***

That summer, I enrolled in two evening classes.

It wasn’t Miss Emily’s idea, though she had left a course catalogue on my desk without comment, a silence more labor-intensive than speech.

Daniel bought me a laptop. I thanked him, then said I would pay for half.

“Why?”

“Otherwise I’ll feel I have to get all A’s.”

He laughed, then saw I meant it.

We were learning. Slowly.

I still visited Bell’s. Six self-checkout machines had replaced two registers. My old supervisor said they were having trouble keeping people.

“Imagine,” I said.

I stood in a staffed line although the machines were empty. The cashier had a silver stud above her lip. She asked whether I wanted a receipt.

For a second, I couldn’t answer.

***

Miss Emily broke her wrist in September on a wet step outside the laundry. She blamed the exterior paint. This may have been true.

Daniel was away. I drove her to the orthopedist, then home.

In her kitchen, she considered the coffee machine as though it were an employee who had disappointed her.

“I can do it,” I said.

“I know you can.”

“Then sit down.”

She looked at me.

I looked back.

Eventually, she sat.

Without her opening things and correcting their placement, the house seemed less like a finished argument and more like somewhere a person lived alone.

I found bread in the freezer. She told me which pan to use for eggs.

“I know how to make eggs, Miss Emily.”

“I didn’t say you didn’t.”

“You were about to.”

She made a sound that might have been a laugh.

We ate at the kitchen table. Her cast was an unexpectedly cheerful pink.

After a while, she said, “You frightened me.”

“When?”

“When Daniel called from City Hall.”

I buttered toast that no longer needed it.

“He does things as though someone will always make them work afterward.”

I remembered his declined card, the groceries between us.

“I do, too,” I said.

“Yes. I’m beginning to see that.”

It wasn’t quite what I meant, but I let it stand.

She followed me to the door. The weather had turned; I had brought out the navy coat that morning.

“Those sleeves are long,” she said.

“They’re fine.”

“Let me see.”

I held out my arms. With her good hand, she folded each cuff inward. The adjustment was slight. I could see my wrists.

“There.”

She waited to see whether I would object. For once, I wasn’t sure whether she was correcting me or helping, and it occurred to me that she might not know either.

I left the cuffs as they were.
